{"id": "1:1/q07", "question": "What governs the opening prepositional phrase?", "turns_on": "Which implicit verb or noun is supplied and whether it precedes or follows the formula.", "positions": [{"id": "1:1/q07/p1", "position": "An omitted verb understood from the action governs the opening phrase.", "reasons": "MAJAZ (author): The verb before bi-smi Allāh is elliptical: the sense is to begin in God’s name before everything and as the first thing. TAB-FULL (author): At Qurʾān recitation the implicit verb is read, while in other acts it is rise, sit, or the relevant action, all begun with God’s name. THALABI (author): The phrase has an omitted command, understood as “say” or “begin” in God’s name. WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The verb governed by bāʾ in the basmala is omitted because context supplies the sense: I began, or begin, in God's name. BAGHAWI (author): The governing verb is omitted and inferred as either “I begin in God's name” or “Say in God's name.” BAGHAWI (author): Another explanation says the elongated bāʾ compensates for the omitted alif; in “Read in your Lord's name” the alif remains, and it is not omitted outside this construction with God's name. | mentions 96:1 BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The prefixed bi- governs what follows; its omitted complement is understood as ‘I begin’ or ‘say’ in God’s name. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Another explanation says the ba was lengthened to mark where the omitted alif had been; the spelling keeps the alif in ‘read in the name of your Lord.’ | mentions 96:1 KASHSHAF (author): The omitted verb follows the basmala because God's name is the focus: fronting it gives exclusive force against beginning in idol names. KASHSHAF (author): The prefixed bā attaches to an omitted verb, understood as I read or recite in God's name. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The preposition bi is attached to an omitted verb such as I read or recite in God's name; the reciter supplies the action begun by the basmala. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The omitted governing verb is placed after the basmala because God's name, the more important element, should come first and signal exclusive invocation of God. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The basmala's omitted verb is illustrated by Arabic prayers for a newly married couple and by a poet's account of being called to a meal. TABRISI (author): The preposition bā originally marks attachment and brings an action onto its object; an implicit verb such as begin or say governs it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Bismillāh is elliptical for I begin or I began in God's name. RAZI-FULL (author): The omitted governor may be a noun or verb and may precede or follow the phrase, yielding four possible constructions. RAZI-FULL (الشيخ أبو بكر الرازي): Abu Bakr al-Razi says the omitted word is an imperative verb, inferred from the nearby command 'You alone we worship'; the implied instruction is 'Say: In God's name.' | mentions 1:5 RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi favors an omitted noun: 'In God's name is the beginning of everything' states that God is intrinsically the source and creator of events, whether or not anyone says it. QURTUBI (نحاة البصرة): Basran grammarians parse bismillah as the predicate of an omitted beginning or as governed by “established” or “fixed.” BAYDAWI (author): The bāʾ attaches to omitted “I read,” since what follows is recited; this is better than “I begin,” unsupported by context, or “my beginning,” requiring extra ellipsis. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The prefixed ب is attached to an omitted verb meaning “I read,” since what follows is read; each actor supplies the verb suited to what the naming begins. NASAFI (author): The basmala’s bā’ attaches to an omitted verb supplied from context, such as ‘I read’ or ‘I recite’; a traveler, slaughterer, or other actor similarly supplies the action being begun. NASAFI-FULL (author): The initial ba attaches to an omitted verb such as “I read” or “I recite”; the act named is understood from the basmala that precedes it, as in a traveler saying it on departure or arrival. NASAFI-FULL (author): The omitted verb follows the basmala because the act and its object matter most; placing the divine name first gives it exclusive priority over the polytheists' invocations of al-Lat and al-Uzza. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): In bismillāh the bāʾ marks instrumentality and the omitted verb is understood as I began; Kufans parse the phrase as an object. SAMIN-DURR (author): Some Kufans place an implicit verb before the phrase; others, including al-Zamakhshari, place it after to mark exclusive dedication against pagan formulas naming al-Lat or al-Uzza. SAMIN-DURR (الفراء): Al-Farra' takes the omitted governing verb as an imperative: you read in God's name. ALUSI (author): The prepositional phrase is “stable” under one terminology because its governing word is omitted; definitions of stable and non-stable adverbials vary by convention. ALUSI-FULL (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir supplies the omitted verb as I recite, since what is recited is the object; Alusi says each speaker supplies the specific action they are beginning, a natural convention that permits basmala to begin the full act. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عربي): Ibn Arabi interprets the phrase esoterically as the predicate of an omitted subject, the world's beginning and manifestation through divine names, and Alusi says objecting to him is unfair. ALUSI-FULL (الرسميون): Calligraphers say the ba is lengthened to represent the omitted alif, compensate for it, and begin scripture with a majestic letter; a report attributes penmanship instructions to the Prophet addressing Muʿawiya. IBNASHUR (author): Omitting the action makes the formula concise and reusable before any deed without altering Qur’anic wording; omitted elements differ from stable adverbs whose governors are never expressed. IBNASHUR (author): The governed element after bi is omitted, here understood as I read; omission is conventional because the basmala accompanies the beginning of good deeds and the intended action supplies the cue. IBNASHUR (author): The phrase is a mobile adverbial dependent on an omitted verb, not a stable predicative adverb; the specific action, rather than a generic begin, is understood. IBNASHUR (author): The omitted verb should name the action being begun, so all of that action is associated with God’s blessing; a generic begin would cover only its first instant. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The omitted complement of “in the name of God” is, here, “I read”; it is conventionally omitted when beginning a good action and recovered from context.
